notes: Crop history timeline. "ago" = about how many years ago people first farmed (domesticated) the crop, counted back from about 2025. Built by tools/build_crophistory.py.

items.name: Fig
items.text: Burnt figs found in an old village may be the oldest farmed fruit. People grew new trees from cuttings. Scientists still argue about this find.

src.t: Kislev, Hartmann & Bar-Yosef 2006, "Early domesticated fig in the Jordan Valley," Science

items.name: Grape
items.text: Grapes were tamed in two places at about the same time: once for eating and once for wine.

src.t: Dong et al. 2023, "Dual domestications and origin of traits in grapevine evolution," Science

items.name: Barley
items.text: Barley was one of the very first crops, grown side by side with wheat.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Lentil
items.text: Lentils were one of the first beans people farmed.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Wheat
items.text: Early farmers kept seeds that stayed on the plant instead of falling off. That made wheat easy to harvest.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Chickpea
items.text: Chickpeas came from a wild plant that grows in only a few hills.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Pea
items.text: Peas were farmed with the first wheat and barley.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Squash and pumpkins
items.text: Squash was tamed more than once. Early squash had small, hard fruits, used for seeds and as cups.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Corn (maize)
items.text: Corn came from a wild grass called teosinte. Its tiny ears grew bigger over thousands of years.

src.t: Piperno et al. 2009, "Starch grain and phytolith evidence for early ninth millennium B.P. maize," PNAS
Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Potato
items.text: All farmed potatoes trace back to one area of the Andes. Thousands of kinds are still grown there.

src.t: Spooner et al. 2005, "A single domestication for potato," PNAS
Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Sugarcane
items.text: People first chewed the sweet stalks. Much later, people in Asia learned to make sugar from the juice.

src.t: Garsmeur et al. 2025, "The genomic footprints of wild Saccharum species trace domestication ... of sugarcane," Cell

items.name: Peach
items.text: Old peach pits found in China got bigger over time. That shows people were picking the best trees.

src.t: Zheng, Crawford & Chen 2014, "Archaeological evidence for peach cultivation and domestication in China," PLOS ONE

items.name: Peanut
items.text: People grew peanuts in South America long before they reached the rest of the world.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Banana
items.text: Farmers in New Guinea grew bananas in swampy gardens. Farmed bananas have tiny seeds or none.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Rice
items.text: Farmers picked rice that held its grains until harvest. Rice was also tamed in India and in Africa.

src.t: Fuller et al. 2009, "The domestication process and domestication rate in rice," Science
Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Tomato
items.region: Mexico (wild ancestors from Ecuador and Peru)
items.text: Small wild tomatoes spread north. In Mexico they became the big tomato we know.

src.t: Razifard et al. 2020, "Genomic evidence for complex domestication history of the cultivated tomato in Latin America," Mol. Biol. Evol.

items.name: Lima bean
items.text: Lima beans got their name from Lima, a city in Peru.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Peppers and chilies
items.text: Peppers were tamed in several places. Bell peppers, jalapeños, habaneros and the hottest chilies all come from these.

src.t: Kraft et al. 2014, "Multiple lines of evidence for the origin of domesticated chili pepper," PNAS
Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Cacao (chocolate)
items.text: Old pots in Ecuador still hold bits of cacao. People used it long before chocolate bars.

src.t: Zarrillo et al. 2018, "The use and domestication of Theobroma cacao during the mid-Holocene in the upper Amazon," Nature Ecology & Evolution

items.name: Common bean
items.text: Green beans and dry beans are the same plant. It was tamed twice, once in Mexico and once in the Andes.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Sorghum
items.text: Sorghum handles heat and dry weather, so it spread across Africa and to India.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Sweet potato
items.text: Sweet potatoes later crossed the Pacific Ocean to islands far away.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Sunflower
items.text: Sunflowers are one of the few big crops first farmed in what is now the United States.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Watermelon
items.text: A painting in an old Egyptian tomb shows a watermelon. Its closest wild cousin grows in Sudan.

src.t: Renner et al. 2021, "A chromosome-level genome of a Kordofan melon illuminates the origin of domesticated watermelons," PNAS

items.name: Melon
items.text: Melons were tamed more than once, in Asia and in Africa.

src.t: Larson et al. 2014, "Current perspectives and the future of domestication studies," PNAS (Fig. 2 timeline)

items.name: Turnip
items.text: Turnips were likely the first crop made from this wild mustard plant. Bok choy came later from the same plant.

src.t: McAlvay et al. 2021, "Brassica rapa domestication," Mol. Biol. Evol.

items.name: Apple
items.text: Wild apples still grow in forests there. Traders carried them along old roads, and grafting kept the best ones.

src.t: Spengler 2019, "Origins of the apple," Frontiers in Plant Science

items.name: Cabbage family
items.text: Kale, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts are all one plant. Kale and cabbage came first. Brussels sprouts came much later.

src.t: Mabry et al. 2021, "The evolutionary history of wild, domesticated, and feral Brassica oleracea," Mol. Biol. Evol.

items.name: Carrot
items.text: The first farmed carrots were purple or yellow. Orange carrots came later.

src.t: Iorizzo et al. 2013, "Genetic structure and domestication of carrot," American Journal of Botany

items.name: Garden strawberry
items.region: France (from two wild strawberries of the Americas)
items.text: Two wild strawberries, one from North America and one from Chile, crossed in a garden in France.

src.t: Edger et al. 2019, "Origin and evolution of the octoploid strawberry genome," Nature Genetics

items.name: Pecan
items.text: Native peoples ate wild pecans for thousands of years. The first grafted pecan orchard was made about 180 years ago.

src.t: USDA-ARS Pecan Breeding & Genetics — Centennial, the first grafted pecan orchard
New Mexico State University Pecan Toolbox — History

items.name: Blueberry
items.text: People picked wild blueberries for a very long time. Growing them on farms started only about 110 years ago.

src.t: Acta Horticulturae 810 (2009), "Domestication of the highbush blueberry at Whitesbog, New Jersey, 1911–1916"
